title: Game design through AI doesn't feel productive and bores me
author: No_Departure7494
selftext:
I see these one shot posts and it just blow my mind. Because, for me - I have to type in "Do this, do this", and it computes (ASTRA) for 45 minutes only to have it 40% of what I asked for. 

It's like your locked in, so I have to scroll on the web, watch youtube, read a book, all while it tries to complete my task. Feels like there should be more time for productivity but there's not.

comments.author: pikuray
comments.body: The stuff people post here name me feel like i suck because I've been prompting for 1 day and half and it still looks like half baked shit!

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body:
Same. I see the best results directly in Claude using whatever engine it provides. I am using Meshy (Which is absolutely terrific), Blender, and then Unity. I want a real game engine, not HTML. It struggles a lot, honestly. The technology is still amazing, but as far as unity goes - it is nowhere near the level of detail that these 'oneshot' Claude posts pump out.

Maybe my philosophy is wrong.

replies.author: EasyTarget973
replies.body: what do your prompts look like?

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body:
I tell Chatgpt - Write a prompt for me which would ask to generate an extremely detailed suburban neighborhood in Blender

It looks good, it does. Again, I am naturally very lazy. If not for AI, this wouldn't be happening, but even then it looks kind of substandard. 

Here's an example. [https://imgur.com/iJMqVoo](https://imgur.com/iJMqVoo)

At a glance, the ability to accomplish this at all is amazing, especially using a satellite photo, but compared to the other games developed on here? Not even one shot - IN A DAY? I simply don't see how it's possible. 

Like, I can't think of a single prompt that would create quality that is 1/10th of what others post.

replies.author: EasyTarget973
replies.body:
you might want try to define 'extremely detailed' a bit better. 'Use PBR Textures, make sure props are added to make the neighborhood feel lived in, etc.'

better: it's way easier to generate 2D concept first, then use that as ref/direction for 3D, then you know what the AI will build, before it does.

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body: Just so I am not delusion - How would you grade that blender creation it built for me? Is it as shit as I think?

replies.author: EasyTarget973
replies.body: looks like a decent foundation to build on, would work for a strategy type game as is, the neighborhood looks like it needs more details like streetlights, sidewalks, etc.

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body:
Absolutely. Again, I just cannot see how it's possible to cram all of that into one prompt.

Not even to one shot it. That is not my goal at all. How you can cram that in to even 1 days worth of computing.

replies.author: EasyTarget973
replies.body:
>How you can cram that in to even 1 days worth of computing.

Unemployed game devs + artists using their expertise lol

replies.author: Blaike325
replies.body: Because a lot of people lie about how much effort they put into their work, lot of claiming “this took 40 minutes” meanwhile they somehow created budget no man’s sky at home somehow. Take however long someone claims something took and multiply that time/prompt amount by at least 4

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
>I have to type in "Do this, do this", and it computes (ASTRA) for 45 minutes only to have it 40% of what I asked for.

Sounds like a prompting or a model issue. I'm using Opus 5.5 and it gets like 90% of the prompt right the first time. Revisions are usually one prompt follow ups.

>The AI almost kinda seem lazy

The length of time it takes depends entirely on what you're asking it to do and how good the model is at doing it. I've had one-shots with Opus take 20 minutes, and some nearly an hour and half. The difference being those 20 minute ones were 4-5 sentences and making a game with SNES graphics while the hour and a half was three pages of mechanics, lore, quests, and other stuff, plus telling it to make something with 3D graphics from scratch.

You're looking at it the wrong way. Put your prompt in, hit send, then fuck off and do other stuff. Go for a walk, play with your pets, ride a bike, lift some weights. We're in an era where you can get work done while you do things we typically neglect because we have to get work done.

comments.author: ElderberryLife5256
comments.body: I think its only some time for this though. Astra did do RL on blender so 3d models are a lot better right now. And the next iterations they may also do the same with Game UIs and then these models can do the stuff on their own. Right now people are using clever workflows to make AI do the stuff.

comments.author: TheCelestialBubble
comments.body: Well I think 99% of the one shot posts are clones of already existing games. It's a lot easier to just clone something already made then create something new.

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body: This is very possible and I think you may be right for the majority of them.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
This is where multiple agents come in. If you have 3-5 agents running simultaneously, as one comes in with a project result, you can immediately be working on checking over its work and giving your feedback as the others continue their work. This used to be pretty unwieldy because they'd get back to you far faster (and have far more errors) but now with how many tokens these models are blasting through with every response, there is plenty of time to juggle.

Alternatively, I also like to hop into Blender and work on models if I don't have a stack of other work to push through.

comments.author: work_guy
comments.body: I can assure you the majority, like all, of the one shot stuff you see here is as hollow as it gets. One scene that barely actually does anything. One shot prompting something should really not be a flex or a goal. It’s taken me over a year to build the workflows, systems (tools supporting the process), skills, conventions etc that produce anything genuinely impressive and playable and they takes weeks and months to get anywhere before I’d even consider showing it to someone. It’s not easy. And it really shouldn’t be honestly, at least in terms of expectations, if you’re interested in making anything of substance. It’s an accelerator, not a replacement for style, patience or effort.

comments.author: GoGs0l0dev
comments.body:
Get another agent and have it do research, start planning our design documents for your other agent…Sol is great for this because it effectively have an infinite limit if you are using codex for your game dev.

I got two other agents going at all time when my primary is on a 20+ minute job to tweak, build, or iterate my game.

comments.author: frogic
comments.body: You should be doing other things while it works.  You should have lots of jobs going at once.  If your plan doesn't allow it have the cheapest models do research or review work.  I'm basically managing 3-4 long workflows at once at all times.  If I have an idea I just try to start work on it.  If those are busy I test work to see if it needs another pass and setup future workflows.

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body: Forgive me ignorance but I am new to this. When you say multiple agents, would that be me typing in multiple prompts under "New Project" or whatever it's titled, separate chats? Or is it just hammering away multiple entries all into the same chat window?

replies.author: frogic
replies.body: I'm doing both.  Right now I'm using my desktop to do heavy jobs so I have a chat with random ideas that assigns it to models on both computers.  If I have a very very novel thing I start a new chat.  If I have 'I don't like the textures on char 2' I usually just toss that into the chat that's sending out jobs so it can queue my resources better.

comments.author: thvaz
comments.body: I enjoyed it more when I had to code more. However, it is insanity to not use it - do I want enjoyment for myself or a finished product?

comments.author: timbo2m
comments.body:
I use two windows machines, one building the game and one I constantly playtest with. I had Claude build a kanban style todo list web UI that saves my change requests I need by level with screenshots into simple todo I commit to git. On the build machine I refresh git and get Claude to build the next todo in "build" status using a build next todo skill that explains the process to a clean run.

This approach allows me to constantly test and queue the next thing I need fixing while Claude builds the last batch of my requests. By the time my play test run finishes, Claude has a new build ready to test and I have a new list of TODO items for claude, so it starts the next round and I playtest the next build. Rinse repeat into infinity
